title: Sugars: oxidation, Fehling's test, invert sugar and the rotation of a mixture
summary: Four benches for four statements: oxidise glucose and gluconic acid with HNO3 and get the same product, run Fehling's on a ketose and watch the copper drop out, hydrolyse sucrose into an equimolar pair, then build the average that turns -40 into -20.
subject: Chemistry
topic: Monosaccharides, reducing sugars and optical rotation
subtopics: Mild versus strong oxidation of glucose
Hydrolysis of sucrose and invert sugar
concepts: A strong oxidant attacks every oxidisable end, not just the reducing one
Alkali converts a ketose into aldoses through a 1,2-enediol
A non-reducing disaccharide has both anomeric carbons tied up
Specific rotation of a mixture is a weighted average, never a sum
Configuration labels and the measured sign of rotation are independent
formulas: mild oxidation (Br2/H2O): CHO -> COOH only, giving gluconic acid
strong oxidation (HNO3): CHO -> COOH and CH2OH -> COOH, giving saccharic acid
enantiomers: specific rotations equal in magnitude, opposite in sign

derivedQuantities.fructose_Fehlings: positive, via the 1,2-enediol to glucose and mannose

methods: Every structure written as SMILES and its functional groups counted by SMARTS matching rather than read off a drawing: glucose returns one aldehyde and one primary alcohol, gluconic acid one carboxyl and one primary alcohol, saccharic acid two carboxyls and no oxidisable end left
That count is what refutes (A): glucose has two ends HNO3 can attack, so it reaches the same dicarboxylic acid that gluconic acid does
Fructose confirmed to contain a ketone and no aldehyde, and the 1,2-enediol confirmed to contain the HO-C=C-OH pattern
Fructose, glucose and mannose all return C6H12O6, confirming the alkaline step is an isomerisation with no atoms gained or lost
Glucose and mannose confirmed to differ at exactly one assigned stereocentre, so the 'another aldohexose' in statement (B) is a specific, real compound
Hydrolysis mass balance: sucrose 342.30 + water 18.02 = 360.31 = glucose 180.16 + fructose 180.16
The two hexoses confirmed to have identical molar mass, which is what makes equimolar equal to equal-mass and legitimises the plain average in (D)
The mixture rotation computed by mass fraction rather than assumed: -20.000 degrees, identical to the simple average of +52.5 and -92.5
The printed distractor reproduced deliberately: +52.5 + (-92.5) = -40 exactly, confirming it is the undivided sum rather than different chemistry
Sign check on the name: sucrose +66.5 is dextrorotatory while the product mixture is laevorotatory, so the rotation inverts - which is what 'invert sugar' records

Answer derived from first principles first; all four verdicts were fixed before any published key was consulted, and then cross-checked against a published answer key and worked solution for this paper, which agree on (B) and (C)

Headless-browser run of the finished page: 71 assertions covering the molecule explorer, both prediction gates refusing to run early, both oxidation flasks, the ketose and the sucrose negative control on Fehling's, the mechanism stepper forwards and back, hydrolysis and the balance, the D/L switch, the tile calculator in both its wrong (-40) and right (-20) configurations, the mixing slider at three compositions, the gate, badges, celebration, traps, progressive hints, teacher mode, theme toggle, clean console and zero horizontal overflow at 390 px and 360 px
verification.note: IIT Roorkee's official key was not retrievable; the published key used for cross-checking is a coaching-institute key that agrees with the independent derivation in every respect.

interactivity: Four separate benches, one per printed statement, each gated behind a prediction the student must commit to before the apparatus will run
Reagent shelf with labelled bottles feeding an oxidation flask, with an animated burner
Clickable Fischer projections: tapping -CHO, -CH2OH, -COOH, an -OH or the enediol carbon explains what that group does under the reagent in use
Oxidation comparison table that refuses to settle statement (A) until both starting materials have been run
Animated test tube: blue Cu(II) solution, bubbles on heating, and a brick-red Cu2O precipitate settling out
Fehling's bench includes a genuine negative control - sucrose stays blue because both anomeric carbons are locked up
Four-step mechanism explorer for the Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein rearrangement with play, pause, step forward and step back, and proper equilibrium harpoons
Sucrose drawn as two rings joined by a clickable glycosidic bond, which splits into two labelled products on hydrolysis by acid or by invertase
Balance showing the 1:1 stoichiometry, with the rotation readout flipping from +66.5 to -20
Working polarimeter: source, polariser, sample tube whose polarisation planes rotate with the reading, analyser and dial
D/L switch that converts the printed L rotations into the D values needed, making the configuration-versus-rotation distinction an action rather than a remark
Mixing chamber slider from pure fructose to pure glucose, with the rotation computed by mass fraction
Tap-to-place tile calculator that lets the student build the wrong answer (-40, undivided) and be told exactly which step is missing before building the right one
Six expandable JEE traps, each phrased as the misconception a student actually holds
Progressive four-level hint system on every bench, conceptual clue first and near-solution last
Progress bar, four earnable badges and an end-of-lab celebration reporting evidence collected and prediction accuracy
Auto play that walks the whole investigation, pausing at each prediction
Teacher mode with objectives, expected wrong answers, a teaching order and a discussion question
Answer gated until all four benches have been run, with a reveal-anyway escape
Step-by-step solution with an independent verification log
